segment.text: 男も女も、その顔にはまだ少しの皺もよってなかった。しかし男の濃い眉毛の陰のくぼんだ優しさうな瞳には、だるさうな疲れの色が見えてゐた。そして女の濃い髪のいろや、細やかな肩のあたりには、なほ打沈んだやうな深い疲れと、まどろむやうな安らかさとが見えてゐた。

segment.text: 彼女は鍋から熱い炊き立ての、白い湯気が一ぱい立ち上ってる御飯をついで彼に渡した。そして彼女の若い大きな瞳も、母親らしい嬉しさにみちて子供の瞬間もぢっとしてない、小鳥のやうに愛らしい様子を見つめた。そして、たまらなささうに、この子はどうしたといふんだらう、とふと口の中に独言を云ひながら、どうにも仕方がない程可愛いといふやうな様子で、『坊や、』と強く云ったけれども、笑が顔からあふれて了って、彼女は助をかりるやうに男の顔を見た。そして三人は、すべての事を忘れてしまった様に、子供の為めに互にどうしようかといふ様に笑ひ合った。そして子供の為めに、彼等は暖かい賑かさと、其上に自然に溢れる笑ひと嬉しさを持って食事にとりかゝったのであった。また彼等は、ごた〳〵した騒がしさの為に、雨風の音を耳にしない。

hard_spots.kind: long cumulative sentences and ruby glosses
hard_spots.why_hard: p8 is one great breath of family laughter; p16 circles with commas and repetition. Chopping into tidy English rationalises the drift, but English breath still needs breaks. Ruby gives readings that change nuance: 怜悧《れいり》, 微笑《ほゝゑみ》, 自然《ひとりで》(= on its own, not 'nature'), 茫然《ぼんやり》, 希《のぞ》み. Translate sense, do not transliterate ruby.

hard_spots.kind: sensory wording that must not become symbol
hard_spots.why_hard: Potato is 凍ったかのやうに固くざくざく, 無味な、かかはりのない冷やかな不味さ. ざくざく is gritty/crunchy hardness, not mealy. かかはりのない means unrelated / having nothing to do with her — the point is its cold ordinariness. Lingering or ennobling it turns it into a symbol the text refuses.

なつかしみと許し and 安らかさ / 安息 recur as a thinking network. 懐しみ is nostalgia/longing for what is past made dear, not homesickness. 許し is forgiveness/pardon. 安息 / 安らかさ is rest/peace, close to but not naming death. Varying them for elegance or clarifying into heaven/old age/premonition would moralise the story.

Child is 女の子 but called 坊や by both parents; English 'boy/sonny' creates a contradiction Japanese passes over. うまうまうまうま with spoon-banging is a nursing baby's 'yum-yum' / food-cry, not words. Needs a neutral warm rendering plus a note, not a quiet fix.

Twice asked why she is silent, she answers with time ('only a short time since we married' / 'only three years') and an unspoken 'large hope she herself does not understand'. Do not bridge into shared understanding; the gap between her far picture and his practical reply is structural.

motifs.english: Keep one plain storm throughout: 'storm' for 嵐, 'sound of rain and wind' for 雨風の音. Let it arrive, disappear under family noise, return to her alone, and close the book, without making it ominous.
motifs.why: Ring-composition: announced in the dark, drowned by lively confusion, heard again by mother alone at the vision, whispered by father over cleared table. It is the world continuing outside the lit room, literal as well as figurative night.

motifs.english: Keep one family of smile-words: smile for 微笑/笑み, laughter for 笑ひ where noisy. Do not vary to grin/beam/smirks. The same smile links present joy and far stillness.
motifs.why: Deliberate network: parents smile over baby now, figures only go on smiling then. Varying destroys the link between warm now and quiet then.

motifs.english: Keep 'far' / 'distant' for every 遠い form, and 'picture' for 絵. She looks at a far place, sees a distant dim picture at the bottom of her eyes and through to the future.
motifs.why: The vision's strangeness is that it is present and distant at once, seen in the same seat. Do not locate it as heaven or memory.

motifs.english: Keep one set: 'quiet' for 静か, 'peace / peaceful' for 安らかさ, 'rest' for 安息. Use the same English each recurrence so the reader hears the return.
motifs.why: Carries the temperature from tired present through vision to final stillness. Elegant variation would flatten the argument that now will become then.

motifs.english: Render なつかしみ consistently as 'nostalgia' (or 'fond longing for what is past' if glossed once) and 許し as 'forgiveness'. Never substitute affection/pardon/mercy in later occurrences.
motifs.why: The story thinks by returning to the same two words: all things will be changed into nostalgia and forgiveness. New synonyms make it sound like new thoughts.

motifs.english: Keep tiredness words together: 'weary / weariness', 'tired', 'drooping'. Preserve the mismatch: no wrinkles yet, but old fatigue.
motifs.why: Text insists twice no wrinkle has come, then loads both bodies with hollow/drooping fatigue. That mismatch is what the potato detonates; ennobling or victimising the parents loses it.

motifs.english: Keep flat repetition: 'day by day' for 一日々々, 'long' for ながい, 'only three years' / 'barely three years'. Leave p14 standing alone as its own paragraph.
motifs.why: Her distortion (a long life already lived, feeling quite old) is measured by the flat correction: barely three years of marriage. Softening that sentence into reflection removes the measure, as does varying 'long'.

narration.english_tense: past as default for the supper action, keeping the vision and its law in the same past-reported present the Japanese uses; do not shift the vision into a separate timeless present or a conditional future that decides what it is
narration.frame: single evening: a small lit room during a storm outside; outwardly nothing changes except serving, feeding, clearing and nursing, while the mother slips inwardly to a far time and returns to practical resolve
narration.narrator: third-person narrator staying close to the young couple, moving most deeply into the wife's interior in p10–p20; sees outward actions plainly and reports her picture and general law in her grammar without certifying what it is
narration.tense_habits: lyrical Taisho past with continuatives (〜てゐた, 〜ている, 〜であった) and present-like general statements; vision passages lengthen into circling present-tense description inside past narration
timeline: p1 dark outside door, storm heard
p2–p9 family gathers at low table under dim lamp; baby bangs spoon, dishes moved under table, rice served, noisy absorption drowns storm
p10–p15 mother serving stew tastes gritty tasteless potato, falls silent, looks far away; rehearses three years of poverty, fear, illness already dreamlike and dear

body.say: This is a single-evening story whose translation stands or falls on holding two times in one prose: the small, poor, noisy present and the mother's dim, still, forgiven far-off time. I am most unsure where English must leave the vision open (three figures, that day, rest like night) without sounding evasive; the margin should say so rather than choose.

style_sheet.annotation_density: sparse; note only what the sentence cannot give: 坊や vs 女の子, アルミ鍋 period poverty, うまうま babble, the 嵐 ring. Never note what context supplies, and never use a note to decode the vision
style_sheet.author_voice: lyrical Taisho prose: soft, lingering, sentimental without irony; long cumulative sentences that drift rather than argue; plain concrete nouns for poor things beside abstract nouns (nostalgia, forgiveness, peace). Resist both drying it out and perfuming it; let flat repetition carry feeling
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: no surnames or given names in text; keep kinship/outward labels as 'the young father' / 'the young mother' / 'the husband' / 'the wife' where Japanese varies 男/父/夫 and 女/母/彼女 — do not normalise to he/she throughout or to modern Mum/Dad. For 坊や versus 女の子 preserve the fork with a note; do not silently fix to 'girl' or 'boy'
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: nothing in romanised body except the baby's うまうま if rendered as 'umma-umma' with a note; render 坊や in English (e.g. 'baby' / 'little one') but flag the literal 'boy' sense in the margin rather than keeping Boy as a name
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese 『』 for speech and ひとり言 to English double quotes; keep husband's two 'why are you silent' and closing soliloquy-like lines as direct speech on their own lines
style_sheet.register: plain literary English, slightly older in feel but prose a good writer would sign; baby scenes warm and concrete, vision passages slow and unadorned; no dialect, no modern slang, no elegant synonyms for repeated words
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: source 《》 are reading glosses, not emphasis: 卓《テーブル》 = table, 自然《ひとりで》 = on its own, etc. Render sense in plain type; do not use italics to carry strangeness unless for the baby's babble if needed

crux.for_the_english: Keep the vision indeterminate and unlabelled: no 'she imagined death', 'in heaven', 'when they were old' where the Japanese does not say it. Preserve the vague deictics and drifting tense — 'that day', 'a day will come' — and let the reader feel, as she does, past and future looking the same from far away. Clarification here (Berman's term) rewrites the story.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on the mother's vision in p16–17 staying a vision, not becoming an explanation. Triggered by a mouthful of badly cooked, almost frozen-tasting potato (p11–12), she drifts into a dim picture of three quiet figures telling an endless story in which all good, evil, sorrow, anger and joy are recounted, yet no one moves — only 'natsukashimi' (longing/nostalgia) and 'forgiveness' and a deep, night-like rest. She herself never names it: it may be old age after a long life, it may be death, it may be simply the far future from which the present will at last look bearable (p17, p20). That refusal to resolve is what turns a scene of poverty into consolation without denying the poverty — they go back to clearing the table and getting up early (p36).
crux.why: The text marks the shift only by soft hedges — 'like a phantom picture' (p15), 'it seemed', 'would surely', repeated 'far away' — and by time collapsing: three years of marriage (p14) already feel like a whole aged life (p13), and are then seen from a distance at which suffering is already 'a nostalgic dream' (p13, p20).

crux.for_the_english: Resist variation and ennoblement: let the same plain English words recur — tired, sorrow, suffering, quiet, peaceful, far away, dream, smile — even where elegant English would vary them, and keep sentences loose and additive rather than tightening them into logical subordination. Keep the dialogue equally plain and slightly bare, especially his rough 'なァ' and her softer forms, without making either quaint dialect.
crux.point: The second crux is the repetitive, incantatory plainness of the narration. The prose does its work by circling the same small stock of words — 疲れ, 悲しみ/苦しみ, 静か, 安らか, 遠い, 微笑, 夢のやう — across the noisy supper, the vision, and the resolve to keep working (p8–35). It is also what holds the opening and close together: the storm unheard in the family's absorption (p8), heard by her inside the vision (p19), and noticed again, quietly, at the end (p38).
crux.why: These are not accidental repetitions to be thinned; they are the network that makes the vision grow out of an ordinary tired evening rather than arrive as an inserted meditation. The couple are explicitly young and unwrinkled (p2–3) yet already exhausted; flat, recurring diction is how that premature weariness sounds.

second.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence from Shiraki's other writing or contemporary commentary that the picture in p16 was a conventional, recognisable image for her first readers (e.g. a specific Buddhist afterlife scene); then a note, though still not an in-text label, might be owed to the reader.

body.why: The 38 paragraphs form one brief continuous supper scene of only a few thousand characters with no chapters or scene breaks, so the whole story is one part a reader can hold whole.

crux.for_the_english: Do not decode the vision for the reader. Do not call it heaven, death, old age, or a premonition, and do not identify the three figures more firmly than the text does. Keep it at the level of a picture seen at the bottom of her eyes, present and distant at once, so the husband's literal reply — counting the years, the baby soon walking — can land beside it without either cancelling the other, and so the closing resolve to work, clear up, and rise early reads as the vision translated into a day's labour rather than explained.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on the mother's inward time-slip, not on the supper. A badly cooked potato — gritty, as if frozen, tasteless — stops the warm, noisy, absorbing present and opens, in the same seat at the same table, onto a far-off time when everything now being lived will have passed and been changed into nostalgia and forgiveness. Only three years of marriage lie behind them, yet under poverty, illness, and material fear they feel like a whole long life already lived and she feels suddenly old; and ahead lies a day, whose nature the text never settles, when that same life will be looked back on in quiet. The crux for the translation is to hold both times in one prose without letting either win: the vivid, tiring now, and the dim, still, forgiven then.
crux.why: Almost everything that matters happens between p10 and p20, inside her, while nothing outwardly changes: she goes on serving beef, onion, carrot and potato, falls silent, looks 'at a far place,' and twice cannot answer her husband. The vision itself (p16–17) is deliberately unlocated — three people in faint dim light, heads together over an endless story in which all the world's good and evil, grief, anger and joy are told, while teller and listener only smile, unmoving, wrapped in nostalgia, forgiveness, and a deep peace. If a fluent version makes that a tidy consolation or a clear afterlife, the story becomes a moral; if it makes her silence mere melancholy or marital distance, the return in p20, smiling at 'what is a day's suffering?', and the practical tenderness of the ending lose their source.

open_questions.question: Who are the three figures in the vision, and what is 'that day' (p20)? The text lets them be the couple and child grown old, the dead at rest, or people in general; the translation should preserve that range, but the editor should note it as an unresolved fork rather than let a rendering quietly choose one.
open_questions.why_it_matters: If the figures are named as the family aged, the vision becomes cosy reminiscence; if named as the dead, it becomes religious consolation. Her peace, and her unexplained smile, depend on it staying a picture, not a doctrine.

open_questions.question: The child is introduced in p2 as a girl (女の子), yet both parents call her 坊や, a word a reader will default to 'boy.' Is this period/familial generic use for a baby, a slip, or a deliberate looseness? A rendering must decide whether to keep a neutral baby-word in English or reproduce 'boy' and create a contradiction the Japanese passes over more lightly.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Introducing 'my boy' in English after 'a girl' makes alert readers stop and suspect an error, pulling attention from scenes whose whole point is unselfconscious absorption in the child.

open_questions.question: How near should 'a rest like night' / being 'before an eternal rest like the night' be allowed to come to death? The storm heard again at p19 and whispered at the close keeps the outside night literal as well as figurative; over- or under-weighting the death register changes the temperature of the final quiet, with the child asleep at the breast.
open_questions.why_it_matters: It decides whether the ending is quietly mortal or simply restful, and therefore how dark the peace she borrows from the future is.

body.reading:
Begin with the ring: a storm outside the door in the dark (p1), unheard through most of the meal because the family's noisy absorption drowns it (p8), heard again by the mother alone at the very moment of her vision (p19), and finally whispered by the father over a cleared table and a sleeping child — 'A storm' (p38). The weather does not symbolise anything the text states; it is the world continuing outside a small lit room, and the translation should let it arrive and return as plainly as that, neither muted at the opening nor made ominous at the close.

The present-tense world of the supper must be kept physically small and poor, because the vision's scale depends on it: a narrow room, a dim lamp hanging by the wall, dishes moved under the table out of a baby's reach, an aluminium pot, rice steaming, beef stewed with onion, carrot and potato in a deep indigo pot. This is not picturesque poverty and should not be ennobled; nor should the parents be made younger-victim figures. The text insists, twice over, that no wrinkle has yet come to either face (p3), that the father still has to be called 'the young father' — and then loads both bodies with a tiredness far beyond that youth: his hollow, gentle eyes, her drooping shoulders, a weariness mixed oddly with a sleepy peace. That mismatch, youth carrying an old fatigue, is what the potato detonates. Her thought in p13–14 — she feels quite old, rehearses tearful days, days frightened by want, days of illness, and finds them already dreamlike and already, startlingly, dear — only works if the correction that follows is left as flat as the text leaves it: looked at, it is barely three years of marriage. Keep that sentence standing alone as a paragraph (p14). Do not soften it into reflection; its flatness is the measure of the distortion.

Her vision needs the most protection from fluency. The sentences of p16 lengthen and circle, repeating 'long,' 'quietly,' 'all' — all the world's good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, trouble, joy — while the figures do almost nothing: they lean in, bow their heads, close their eyes, go on smiling. Then p17 widens from the picture to a general law, in her mind's grammar rather than in narrated certainty: the world's things, life, will pass, and only on the day they have passed will everything be changed into nostalgia and forgiveness, before an eternal rest like night. Render the triad — nostalgia/longing for what is past, forgiveness, peace/rest — consistently each time it recurs (p16, p17, p18, p20), because the text thinks by returning to those same words, not by finding new ones. The same discipline applies to her refrains 'day by day' and 'long' in p20, and to the small repeated actions around the vision: looking far away, falling silent, smiling, sighing. Varying these for English elegance would destroy the network that holds the piece together; the strangeness is that she keeps seeing the same far place and the same picture, and the prose should be allowed to say so in the same words.

Note how little of this she can say aloud. Twice the husband asks why she is silent (p19, p21); twice the answer evades: it is really only a short time since they married; but then, only three years have passed. She is asking him, the text says, to remember everything, back to before the marriage, and what she actually wants to tell him — some large hope she herself does not understand (p27) — never gets spoken. He answers in the only register he has: two years gone, the baby will walk soon, 'just a little longer' (p34), said strongly, like a soliloquy. Do not bridge that gap with connective tissue or a moment of shared understanding; the couple rejoin not by exchanging the vision but side by side in resolve — 'we shall work,' clearing up, sleeping, rising early (p35–36). Her calm at the end is borrowed from a future he has not seen, and the pathos depends on the reader knowing it and him not.

For the English register: this is lyrical Taishō prose, soft, lingering and sentimental in a way modern English will want to dry out or, conversely, to perfume. Resist both. The long cumulative sentences, especially the great single breath of p8 and the circling of p16, should not all be chopped into tidy units — that would be rationalisation, and the drift is the consciousness — but they must remain prose a good writer would sign, so break where English breath genuinely fails rather than where Japanese punctuation happens to sit. Keep the baby scenes noisy and concrete (spoon banged on table, the cry of 'umma-umma,' rice hastily pushed into the father's own mouth while he feeds her) at full, unembarrassed warmth; they are the counterweight, and if they are made cute or cut back for dignity the mother's stillness has nothing to deepen against. The likeliest fluent failures, in order: clarifying the vision into a stated heaven or old age; turning the potato into a symbol by lingering on it, when the text's point is its unrelated, cold, tasteless ordinariness ('no connection' is in the sentence, p12); varying the repeated words for smile, quiet, far and tired; and tidying her non-answers into communication. Where fidelity and ease pull apart, keep the text's vagueness and let the flat, exact repetition carry it.
body.say: The crux is the mother's time-slip at the table. Triggered by nothing more symbolic than a gritty, tasteless potato, three years of poor married life suddenly feel like a whole lifetime already lived — and she sees, dimly, a far day when all of it, suffering included, will have turned into nostalgia, forgiveness and rest. A translation stands or falls on keeping that vision unresolved (neither heaven, nor old age, nor mere daydream), on leaving her unable to tell her husband any of it, and on letting the family's return to work, clearing up and sleep be the only answer the story gives. Around that, hold the ring of the storm, the poverty of the small lit room, and the text's repeated words — smile, quiet, far away, day by day — exactly as repetitions.

items.english: Outside the door, dark now without anyone noticing, came the sound of fierce rain and wind. It was a {t:storm}.

The family had gathered at the {t:table} under the dim {t:lamp} hanging by the wall of the narrow room, about to have their evening meal. The father and mother were both still really young. And the child was a fat little girl, round all over, just able to stand by holding on to the {t:table}.

Neither the man nor the woman had yet a single wrinkle on their faces. But in the man's sunken, gentle-looking eyes, in the shadow of his thick eyebrows, there was a colour of listless weariness. And in the woman's dark hair, and around her slender shoulders, there was a deeper weariness still, as if sunk down, and a peace like dozing.

revision.english: Outside the door, dark by now, there was the sound of hard rain and wind. A storm.

The parents and the child had gathered about the table under the dim electric light hanging close by the wall of the narrow room, about to take their supper. Father and mother were both still truly young. And the child was a round-eyed, plump little girl, just able to stand by holding on to the table.

Neither the man nor the woman had yet a single wrinkle in the face. But in his hollowed, gentle eyes in the shadow of his thick eyebrows there was a look of languid weariness. And about the dark colour of her thick hair and her slender shoulders there lay a still deeper, weighed-down weariness, and a drowsy sort of peace.
The day had ended. The sorrow and suffering of that day were as if about to flow away into the peace of the night. And, smiling in silence, they bent all their gaze upon the child.

Standing as if she might topple, the child kept trying, with fat round arms short as balls, without a moment's gap and far too fast, to sweep at everything on the table. So, still smiling, they set all the bowls and the teapot and the aluminium pan and the rest underneath the table. On the table there was left only the little spoon the child held and a single small dish.
But the child raised a noisy cry full of small delight and banged spoon and dish down upon the table.

"You naughty thing." The young father gazed at the small round arms, and at the child's long, dark-lashed eyes moving busily and sharply without a pause, as if wondering what was to be done, and then with a smile filling his whole face, pinching the child's round thrust-out cheek lightly with his fingers, he felt under the table for a large bowl and put it into her little hands.
notes: 彼女の手 here is the baby's hands, not the mother's; rendered as "her little hands" to keep the reference clear.

revision.english: She served the rice, just cooked and hot from the pot with white steam rising thick, and handed it to him. And her young large eyes too, full of a mother's gladness, gazed at the child, never still for an instant, lovely as a little bird. And as if she could bear it no longer, murmuring under her breath, whatever shall we do with this child, looking for all the world helplessly fond, she said, "Baby," firmly, but the smile overflowed her face, and she looked at the man as if asking for help. And the three laughed together, as if they had forgotten everything, as if wondering what to do for the child. And for the child they fell to their meal, with a warm bustle and with laughter and gladness welling up of themselves. And for all their clattering noise they did not hear the sound of the rain and wind.
notes: 坊や is literally a word for 'boy,' though the child was introduced as a girl in p2; both parents use it as baby-talk address. Rendered here as neutral "Baby" to preserve the fork without deciding it in English.

revision.english: The young father kept his big red hand spread busily over the table. And holding back the smile the child made well up in him in spite of himself, he steadied the child and put a little food into her small red mouth. In the gaps, hastily opening his own wide mouth, he thrust rice into it.

The mother, close by the wall, bowed in silence as she heaped onto white plates the beef and onion, the carrot and the potato stewed in the deep indigo pot. And meaning to say something, she put a sweet, softly stewed potato into her mouth and looked at the man's face, but as if she had noticed something, she shut her mouth and stared vacantly at a far place.

The potato in her mouth was hard and gritty, as if it had been frozen, and tasted very bad. As if taken by surprise, she bit it over again in silence with her front teeth, but her heart had already sunk and bowed itself in loneliness.
notes: ざくざく is a dry, gritty hardness, not mealiness; I keep it as gritty to leave the potato cold and ordinary rather than symbolic.

revision.english: She remembered the suffering and sorrow and weariness of each day. And the tasteless, cold badness of the potato, having no connection with her, gave her a quiet, lonely, far-removed heart. She pictured the poor, sorrow-filled real life since their marriage.
notes: かかはりのない is kept as having no connection, which is the point: the bad taste is unrelated and cold, not a symbol.

revision.english: And it seemed to her like a life dragged on for far too long. She suddenly thought she had grown quite old. And with a distant heart she quietly remembered the quiet days filled with tears, and the days spent threatened and afraid for want of material things, and each day of sorrow and suffering through illness. Yet to her remembering now, it was all like a dream. Suffering and sorrow alike were like a dear, nostalgic dream.
notes: なつかしい is kept as nostalgic to hold the network that returns in the vision.

revision.english: And when she came to think of it, it was no more than barely three years of life since their marriage.
notes: Left flat and standing alone, as in the Japanese, to measure her distortion.

revision.english: Before she knew it, as if her heed had been taken by something, she gazed vacantly far away. Her quiet heart was already seeing a picture as in a vision.

It was in a faint dim light, and three people, quiet as that light, had drawn close and put their heads together and were telling a long story. The story seemed to go on between them, too long ever to come to an end. And in that story seemed to be told everything, all the good and evil in the world, grief and suffering and anger and trouble, joy, everything. But teller and listener alike only went on smiling, quietly and peacefully, with a fixed gaze, and they did not move at all. With heads inclined and eyes lowered, there only a quiet nostalgia and forgiveness seemed to enfold them. And there too a deep, deep peace showed itself in all of them.
notes: Kept the three figures unidentified and the telling almost motionless, holding quiet, smile, nostalgia, forgiveness and peace in the same words used elsewhere. No em dash in source, so none in English.

revision.english: All things in the world, life itself, would pass. And only on the day they had passed would everything, all things, be changed into nostalgia and forgiveness. And then they would be forever before a rest like night.
notes: Kept the general law in past reported form and in the same triad words as p16, without deciding what that day or that rest is.

revision.english: The distant picture lay dark and quiet at the bottom of her eyes. And through the bottom of her eyes, far off in the future, with a lonely peace, that picture was still to be seen. The young woman sighed a lonely hidden sigh alone, and glancing at the littered table and at the faces of her husband and child, she said nothing.
notes: Kept distant for every far form and picture for絵, and quiet, lonely, peace and sigh in the same wording as the surrounding pages.

revision.english: "Why are you silent?" The man looked at the woman's face with a puzzled look and called to her. Hurrying to say something, she found she could say nothing all at once and fell silent, and again her eyes ran far away. And she saw the phantom picture again. Then for the first time she quietly heard the sound of the storm outside the door. She said nothing.

Yes. There was that day. There was the day when all would be changed into nostalgia and forgiveness, and peace. After a long life, and after long sorrow again, and after long suffering again, on the day beyond them, there would be that peaceful day of nostalgia and forgiveness. What were the suffering and sorrow of day by day? What were the weariness and trouble of day by day? Before she knew it she was wearing a smile.
notes: The circling repetition of long and of day by day, and the fixed wording nostalgia and forgiveness, and peace, mirror the Japanese; the stiffness is the text's own return to the same words.

revision.english: "Why are you silent?" the man called to her again. She lifted her head as if startled and, smiling with nostalgia, said, "It has really been only such a short time since we married, hasn't it," as if asking him to remember too, to remember all sorts of things, even the happy things from before they married.
"Yes," the man too lifted his eyes and said, "It is only three years after all. But we have been through a good deal, you and I."

options.case: - The story stands or falls on the mother's inward time-slip, not on the supper. A badly cooked potato — gritty, as if frozen, tasteless — stops the warm, noisy, absorbing present and opens, in the same seat at the same table, onto a far-off time when everything now being lived will have passed and been changed into nostalgia and forgiveness. Only three years of marriage lie behind them, yet under poverty, illness, and material fear they feel like a whole long life already lived and she feels suddenly old; and ahead lies a day, whose nature the text never settles, when that same life will be looked back on in quiet. The crux for the translation is to hold both times in one prose without letting either win: the vivid, tiring now, and the dim, still, forgiven then. Almost everything that matters happens between p10 and p20, inside her, while nothing outwardly changes: she goes on serving beef, onion, carrot and potato, falls silent, looks 'at a far place,' and twice cannot answer her husband. The vision itself (p16–17) is deliberately unlocated — three people in faint dim light, heads together over an endless story in which all the world's good and evil, grief, anger and joy are told, while teller and listener only smile, unmoving, wrapped in nostalgia, forgiveness, and a deep peace. If a fluent version makes that a tidy consolation or a clear afterlife, the story becomes a moral; if it makes her silence mere melancholy or marital distance, the return in p20, smiling at 'what is a day's suffering?', and the practical tenderness of the ending lose their source. Keep it at the level of a picture seen at the bottom of her eyes, present and distant at once, so the husband's literal reply — counting the years, the baby soon walking — can land beside it without either cancelling the other, and so the closing resolve to work, clear up, and rise early reads as the vision translated into a day's labour rather than explained.

payload.say: This is a single-evening story whose translation stands or falls on holding two times in one prose: the small, poor, noisy present and the mother's dim, still, forgiven far-off time. I am most unsure where English must leave the vision open (three figures, that day, rest like night) without sounding evasive; the margin should say so rather than choose.
Drafted the opening storm and supper tableau, keeping the small poor interior and unwrinkled yet weary parents plain.

payload.english: Outside the door, dark by now, there was the sound of hard rain and wind. A storm.

The parents and the child had gathered about the table under the dim electric light hanging close by the wall of the narrow room, about to take their supper. Father and mother were both still truly young. And the child was a round-eyed, plump little girl, just able to stand by holding on to the table.

Neither the man nor the woman had yet a single wrinkle in the face. But in his hollowed, gentle eyes in the shadow of his thick eyebrows there was a look of languid weariness. And about the dark colour of her thick hair and her slender shoulders there lay a still deeper, weighed-down weariness, and a drowsy sort of peace.
The day had ended. The sorrow and suffering of that day were as if about to flow away into the peace of the night. And, smiling in silence, they bent all their gaze upon the child.

Standing as if she might topple, the child kept trying, with fat round arms short as balls, without a moment's gap and far too fast, to sweep at everything on the table. So, still smiling, they set all the bowls and the teapot and the aluminium pan and the rest underneath the table. On the table there was left only the little spoon the child held and a single small dish.
But the child raised a noisy cry full of small delight and banged spoon and dish down upon the table.

payload.say: Drafted p7 to p9 keeping the long meal-breath and smile words together.

payload.english: "You naughty thing." The young father gazed at the small round arms, and at the child's long, dark-lashed eyes moving busily and sharply without a pause, as if wondering what was to be done, and then with a smile filling his whole face, pinching the child's round thrust-out cheek lightly with his fingers, he felt under the table for a large bowl and put it into her little hands.
notes: 彼女の手 here is the baby's hands, not the mother's; rendered as "her little hands" to keep the reference clear.

payload.english: She served the rice, just cooked and hot from the pot with white steam rising thick, and handed it to him. And her young large eyes too, full of a mother's gladness, gazed at the child, never still for an instant, lovely as a little bird. And as if she could bear it no longer, murmuring under her breath, whatever shall we do with this child, looking for all the world helplessly fond, she said, "Baby," firmly, but the smile overflowed her face, and she looked at the man as if asking for help. And the three laughed together, as if they had forgotten everything, as if wondering what to do for the child. And for the child they fell to their meal, with a warm bustle and with laughter and gladness welling up of themselves. And for all their clattering noise they did not hear the sound of the rain and wind.
notes: 坊や is literally a word for 'boy,' though the child was introduced as a girl in p2; both parents use it as baby-talk address. Rendered here as neutral "Baby" to preserve the fork without deciding it in English.

payload.english: The mother, close by the wall, bowed in silence as she heaped onto white plates the beef and onion, the carrot and the potato stewed in the deep indigo pot. And meaning to say something, she put a sweet, softly stewed potato into her mouth and looked at the man's face, but as if she had noticed something, she shut her mouth and stared vacantly at a far place.

The potato in her mouth was hard and gritty, as if it had been frozen, and tasted very bad. As if taken by surprise, she bit it over again in silence with her front teeth, but her heart had already sunk and bowed itself in loneliness.

payload.english: It was in a faint dim light, and three people, quiet as that light, had drawn close and put their heads together and were telling a long story. The story seemed to go on between them, too long ever to come to an end. And in that story seemed to be told everything, all the good and evil in the world, grief and suffering and anger and trouble, joy, everything. But teller and listener alike only went on smiling, quietly and peacefully, with a fixed gaze, and they did not move at all. payload.english: "Why are you silent?" The man looked at the woman's face with a puzzled look and called to her. Hurrying to say something, she found she could say nothing all at once and fell silent, and again her eyes ran far away. And she saw the phantom picture again. Then for the first time she quietly heard the sound of the storm outside the door. She said nothing.

Yes. There was that day. There was the day when all would be changed into nostalgia and forgiveness, and peace. After a long life, and after long sorrow again, and after long suffering again, on the day beyond them, there would be that peaceful day of nostalgia and forgiveness. What were the suffering and sorrow of day by day? What were the weariness and trouble of day by day? Before she knew it she was wearing a smile.
notes: The circling repetition of long and of day by day, and the fixed wording nostalgia and forgiveness, and peace, mirror the Japanese; the stiffness is the text's own return to the same words.

crux.for_the_english: Do not decode the vision for the reader. Do not call it heaven, death, old age, or a premonition, and do not identify the three figures more firmly than the text does. Keep it at the level of a picture seen at the bottom of her eyes, present and distant at once, so the husband's literal reply — counting the years, the baby soon walking — can land beside it without either cancelling the other, and so the closing resolve to work, clear up, and rise early reads as the vision translated into a day's labour rather than explained.
crux.point: The story stands or falls on the mother's inward time-slip, not on the supper. A badly cooked potato — gritty, as if frozen, tasteless — stops the warm, noisy, absorbing present and opens, in the same seat at the same table, onto a far-off time when everything now being lived will have passed and been changed into nostalgia and forgiveness. Only three years of marriage lie behind them, yet under poverty, illness, and material fear they feel like a whole long life already lived and she feels suddenly old; and ahead lies a day, whose nature the text never settles, when that same life will be looked back on in quiet. The crux for the translation is to hold both times in one prose without letting either win: the vivid, tiring now, and the dim, still, forgiven then.
crux.why: Almost everything that matters happens between p10 and p20, inside her, while nothing outwardly changes: she goes on serving beef, onion, carrot and potato, falls silent, looks 'at a far place,' and twice cannot answer her husband. The vision itself (p16–17) is deliberately unlocated — three people in faint dim light, heads together over an endless story in which all the world's good and evil, grief, anger and joy are told, while teller and listener only smile, unmoving, wrapped in nostalgia, forgiveness, and a deep peace. If a fluent version makes that a tidy consolation or a clear afterlife, the story becomes a moral; if it makes her silence mere melancholy or marital distance, the return in p20, smiling at 'what is a day's suffering?', and the practical tenderness of the ending lose their source.

open_questions.question: Who are the three figures in the vision, and what is 'that day' (p20)? The text lets them be the couple and child grown old, the dead at rest, or people in general; the translation should preserve that range, but the editor should note it as an unresolved fork rather than let a rendering quietly choose one.
open_questions.why_it_matters: If the figures are named as the family aged, the vision becomes cosy reminiscence; if named as the dead, it becomes religious consolation. Her peace, and her unexplained smile, depend on it staying a picture, not a doctrine.

open_questions.question: The child is introduced in p2 as a girl (女の子), yet both parents call her 坊や, a word a reader will default to 'boy.' Is this period/familial generic use for a baby, a slip, or a deliberate looseness? A rendering must decide whether to keep a neutral baby-word in English or reproduce 'boy' and create a contradiction the Japanese passes over more lightly.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Introducing 'my boy' in English after 'a girl' makes alert readers stop and suspect an error, pulling attention from scenes whose whole point is unselfconscious absorption in the child.

open_questions.question: How near should 'a rest like night' / being 'before an eternal rest like the night' be allowed to come to death? The storm heard again at p19 and whispered at the close keeps the outside night literal as well as figurative; over- or under-weighting the death register changes the temperature of the final quiet, with the child asleep at the breast.
open_questions.why_it_matters: It decides whether the ending is quietly mortal or simply restful, and therefore how dark the peace she borrows from the future is.

reading.reading:
Begin with the ring: a storm outside the door in the dark (p1), unheard through most of the meal because the family's noisy absorption drowns it (p8), heard again by the mother alone at the very moment of her vision (p19), and finally whispered by the father over a cleared table and a sleeping child — 'A storm' (p38). The weather does not symbolise anything the text states; it is the world continuing outside a small lit room, and the translation should let it arrive and return as plainly as that, neither muted at the opening nor made ominous at the close.

The present-tense world of the supper must be kept physically small and poor, because the vision's scale depends on it: a narrow room, a dim lamp hanging by the wall, dishes moved under the table out of a baby's reach, an aluminium pot, rice steaming, beef stewed with onion, carrot and potato in a deep indigo pot. This is not picturesque poverty and should not be ennobled; nor should the parents be made younger-victim figures. The text insists, twice over, that no wrinkle has yet come to either face (p3), that the father still has to be called 'the young father' — and then loads both bodies with a tiredness far beyond that youth: his hollow, gentle eyes, her drooping shoulders, a weariness mixed oddly with a sleepy peace. That mismatch, youth carrying an old fatigue, is what the potato detonates. Her thought in p13–14 — she feels quite old, rehearses tearful days, days frightened by want, days of illness, and finds them already dreamlike and already, startlingly, dear — only works if the correction that follows is left as flat as the text leaves it: looked at, it is barely three years of marriage. Keep that sentence standing alone as a paragraph (p14). Do not soften it into reflection; its flatness is the measure of the distortion.

Her vision needs the most protection from fluency. The sentences of p16 lengthen and circle, repeating 'long,' 'quietly,' 'all' — all the world's good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, trouble, joy — while the figures do almost nothing: they lean in, bow their heads, close their eyes, go on smiling. Then p17 widens from the picture to a general law, in her mind's grammar rather than in narrated certainty: the world's things, life, will pass, and only on the day they have passed will everything be changed into nostalgia and forgiveness, before an eternal rest like night. Render the triad — nostalgia/longing for what is past, forgiveness, peace/rest — consistently each time it recurs (p16, p17, p18, p20), because the text thinks by returning to those same words, not by finding new ones. The same discipline applies to her refrains 'day by day' and 'long' in p20, and to the small repeated actions around the vision: looking far away, falling silent, smiling, sighing. Varying these for English elegance would destroy the network that holds the piece together; the strangeness is that she keeps seeing the same far place and the same picture, and the prose should be allowed to say so in the same words.

Note how little of this she can say aloud. Twice the husband asks why she is silent (p19, p21); twice the answer evades: it is really only a short time since they married; but then, only three years have passed. She is asking him, the text says, to remember everything, back to before the marriage, and what she actually wants to tell him — some large hope she herself does not understand (p27) — never gets spoken. He answers in the only register he has: two years gone, the baby will walk soon, 'just a little longer' (p34), said strongly, like a soliloquy. Do not bridge that gap with connective tissue or a moment of shared understanding; the couple rejoin not by exchanging the vision but side by side in resolve — 'we shall work,' clearing up, sleeping, rising early (p35–36). Her calm at the end is borrowed from a future he has not seen, and the pathos depends on the reader knowing it and him not.

For the English register: this is lyrical Taishō prose, soft, lingering and sentimental in a way modern English will want to dry out or, conversely, to perfume. Resist both. The long cumulative sentences, especially the great single breath of p8 and the circling of p16, should not all be chopped into tidy units — that would be rationalisation, and the drift is the consciousness — but they must remain prose a good writer would sign, so break where English breath genuinely fails rather than where Japanese punctuation happens to sit. Keep the baby scenes noisy and concrete (spoon banged on table, the cry of 'umma-umma,' rice hastily pushed into the father's own mouth while he feeds her) at full, unembarrassed warmth; they are the counterweight, and if they are made cute or cut back for dignity the mother's stillness has nothing to deepen against. The likeliest fluent failures, in order: clarifying the vision into a stated heaven or old age; turning the potato into a symbol by lingering on it, when the text's point is its unrelated, cold, tasteless ordinariness ('no connection' is in the sentence, p12); varying the repeated words for smile, quiet, far and tired; and tidying her non-answers into communication. Where fidelity and ease pull apart, keep the text's vagueness and let the flat, exact repetition carry it.
reading.say: The crux is the mother's time-slip at the table. Triggered by nothing more symbolic than a gritty, tasteless potato, three years of poor married life suddenly feel like a whole lifetime already lived — and she sees, dimly, a far day when all of it, suffering included, will have turned into nostalgia, forgiveness and rest. A translation stands or falls on keeping that vision unresolved (neither heaven, nor old age, nor mere daydream), on leaving her unable to tell her husband any of it, and on letting the family's return to work, clearing up and sleep be the only answer the story gives. Around that, hold the ring of the storm, the poverty of the small lit room, and the text's repeated words — smile, quiet, far away, day by day — exactly as repetitions.

student.ja: そして、それがあまりに永く引きつゞいた生活のやうにも思はれた。彼女はふと自分がすっかり老いてしまったかのやうに考へられた。そして静かに涙にみちた日のことや、物質の為めに脅かされ恐れてすごした日々や、病の為めに悲しみ苦しんだその日その日のことを遠い心が静かに思出してゐるのだった。けれどもいま思出してる彼女には、すべてが夢のやうであった。苦しみも悲しみもなつかしい夢のやうであった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: And when she came to think of it, it was no more than barely three years of life since their marriage.
student.ja: そして考へて見れば、わづかに結婚後の三年ばかりの生活にすぎない。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: Before she knew it, as if her attention had been caught by something, she gazed vacantly far away. Her quiet heart was already seeing a picture as in a vision.
student.ja: 彼女は、いつとなく何物にか気をとられたやうに、ぼんやりと遠くの方を見てゐた。彼女のその静かな心が、いつか幻のやうな絵を見てゐたのであった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: It was in a faint dim light, and three people, quiet as that light, had drawn close and put their heads together and were telling a long story. The story seemed to go on between them, too long ever to come to an end. And in that story seemed to be told everything, all the good and evil in the world, grief and suffering and anger and trouble, joy, everything. But teller and listener alike only went on smiling, quietly and peacefully, steadily, and they did not move at all. With heads inclined and eyes lowered, there only a quiet nostalgia and forgiveness seemed to enfold them. And there too a deep, deep peace showed itself in all of them.
student.ja: それは淡暗い光りのなかに、そしてその光りのやうに物静かな三人の人たちが、より合って頭をあつめてながい物語りをしてゐるのだった。その物語りは、あまりにながく絶えることなく彼等の間につゞけられてゐるやうであった。そしてその物語りのなかには、すべて世の中の善や悪や、かなしみや苦しみ怒りもなやみも、よろこびもすべてが語られてるやうだった。けれども話す人も聞く人も、たゞ静かに安らかにぢっと微笑をつゞけてゐるばかりであって、彼等は少しも動かなかった。首をかたむけて眼を伏せながら、そして、そこにはたゞ静かななつかしみと、許しとが彼等をつつんでゐるやうに見えた。そしてまたそこには深い〳〵安らかさが彼等のすべてに表はれてゐるのであった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: All things in the world, life itself, would pass. And only on the day they had passed would everything, all things, change into nostalgia and forgiveness. And then they would stand forever before a rest like night.
student.ja: 世の中の總ての事、人生は過去るであらう。そして過去った其日に初めて總てが、總ての事が懐しみと許しとに変る事だらう。そして其時彼等は永久に夜の様な安息の前にあるのであった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The distant picture lay dark and quiet at the bottom of her eyes. And through the bottom of her eyes, far off in the future, with a lonely peace, that picture was still to be seen. The young woman, on her own, sighed a lonely hidden sigh, and glancing at the littered table and at the faces of her husband and child, she said nothing.
student.ja: 遠い絵が暗く静かに、彼女の眼の底に映ってゐた。また瞳の底を通して遠く未来に、淋しい安らかさを持って、その絵が見えるのであった。若い彼女は一人で淋しいひそかな溜息をついた、そして、とり散らされたテーブルの上と、夫と子供の顔をちらと見ながら黙ってゐた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Why are you silent?" The man looked at the woman's face with a puzzled look and called to her. Hurrying to say something, she found she could say nothing all at once and fell silent, and again her eyes strayed far away. And she saw the phantom picture again. Then for the first time she quietly heard the sound of the storm outside the door. She said nothing.
student.ja: 『どうして黙ってるの。』男は、ふと不思議さうに女の顔を見て声をかけた。彼女は、あわてゝなにかを云はうとしたが、一口には何事も云ひかねて黙ってしまふと、再びその眼が遠く走ってしまった。そして彼女は、また幻の絵を見たのだった。彼女は、その時はじめて戸の外の嵐の音を、静かに耳にした。彼女はなにも云はずにゐた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: Yes. There is that day. There is the day when all changes into nostalgia and forgiveness, and peace. After a long life, and after long sorrow again, and after long suffering again, on the day beyond them, there is that peaceful day of nostalgia and forgiveness. What are the suffering and sorrow of day by day? What are the weariness and trouble of day by day? Before she knew it she was wearing a smile.
student.ja: さうだ。あの日があるのだ。あのすべてがなつかしみと許しと、安らかさに変る日があるのだった。ながい生活の後に、またながい悲しみの後に、またながい苦しみのその後の日に、あの安らかななつかしみと許しの日があるのだ。一日々々の苦しみや悲しみがなんだらう。一日々々の疲れやなやみがなんだらう。彼女はいつとなしに微笑を浮べてゐた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Why are you silent?" the man called to her again. She lifted her head as if startled and, smiling with nostalgia, said, "It has really been only such a short time since we married, hasn't it," as if asking him to remember too, to remember all sorts of things, even the happy things from before they married.
student.ja: 『なぜ黙ってるの。』男は再び声をかけた。彼女は驚いたやうに頭を上げて、なつかしさうに笑ひながら、
student.label: house-checked

student.ja: 『まだ本当にわづかしか経ちませんのね、結婚してから。』
student.label: house-checked

student.ja: と男にも思出して、種々のことを、結婚前の楽しかったことまでも、思出して下さいと云ふやうに云った。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Yes," the man too lifted his eyes and said, "It is only three years after all. But we've been through a lot, we have."
student.ja: 『さうだなァ。』男も眼を上げて云った。
student.label: house-checked

student.ja: 『たった三年にしかならないんだな。けれども、俺たちはいろ〳〵苦労したなァ。』
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Indeed," she said, lowering her eyes again as if to look at that picture. But at once, "But it is only three years since then, after all," her eyes shone as if she must tell him of some great hope, some great hope she herself did not understand.
student.ja: 『本当にね。』彼女は、また眼を伏せてあの絵を見ようとした。が、すぐに、
student.label: house-checked

student.ja: 『けれども、まだ三年しか経たないんですものね。』と、なにか大きな、彼女にはわからないけれども、なにか大きな希みを彼に話さなければならないやうに瞳を輝かした。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Yes, though day by day this and that wears us out and troubles us and makes us suffer, two years are past already. In a little while our baby will be walking."
student.ja: 『さうだ、一日々々いろ〳〵なことに疲らされなやまされ苦しまされても、二年はもう過ぎたんだからな。もうしばらくすると、坊やも歩るくやうになるんだから。』
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The man looked at the child standing there holding the spoon idly. At once the mother called out gladly in a loud voice, "Baby!" and at the same moment the child raised a loud cry and, looking into her mother's face, banged the spoon upon the table, "Umma-umma-umma-umma."
student.ja: 男は、手持ぶさたのやうにスプーンを持って立ってる子供を見た。彼女は、すぐに嬉しさうに、
student.label: house-checked

student.ja: 『坊や。』と大きな声を出した、子供はそれと同時に大きな叫声を上げて、母親の顔を見ながら、
student.label: house-checked

student.ja: 『うま〳〵〳〵〳〵。』とスプーンをテーブルにたゝきつけた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: The father hastily put rice into the child's mouth.
student.ja: 父親は、あわてゝ子供の口に御飯を入れてやった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: Presently they laid down their chopsticks.
student.ja: 彼等は、やがて箸をおいた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Only a little longer," the man said strongly, as if to himself.
student.ja: 『もう少しの間だ。』男は強く独言のやうに云った。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Yes, we shall work," she said, calm and peaceful. And holding the child upon her knees, she put out her small nipple and began to nurse her.
student.ja: 『さうね、私たちは働きませうね。』彼女は、おちついて安らかに云った。そして子供を膝の上に抱きながら、小さな乳首をだして乳をのませ初めた。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "Come, let us clear away what is left. And let us sleep. Tomorrow let us rise early."
student.ja: 『さ、あとを片づけよう。そして寝よう、明日は早く起きようぢゃないか。』
student.label: house-checked

student.en: Presently the man stood up. And as he began to clear the table, the child had already closed her eyes with her cheek against the breast. All about them was quiet.
student.ja: やがて、男は立ち上った。そしてテーブルを片づけ初めようとした時、もはや子供は乳房に頬をつけて眼を閉ぢてゐた。あたりは静まりかへった。
student.label: house-checked

student.en: "A storm," the man said, standing still, in a whisper.
student.ja: 『嵐だな。』男は、立ちどまってさゝやいた。
student.label: house-checked
